analysis.body:
# Government AI Sector Analysis

Federal agencies across the United States are deploying artificial intelligence at an early stage, with substantial planned growth still ahead. According to GAO audits, twenty of twenty-three federal agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, though most remain in planning phases rather than active production. In approximately 200 instances, agencies reported currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases. Agency-reported applications include analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing drone photographs, and targeting of scientific specimens for planetary rovers. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI, signaling federal commitment to the technology.

Implementation across agencies is incomplete and inconsistent. GAO found that ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, while twelve implemented some but not all. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, but fifteen had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data. Some inventories lacked required data elements such as AI life cycle stage or whether a use case was releasable, and two inventories included uses later determined not to be AI. Without accurate inventories, the government's management of its use of AI is hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data, according to GAO.

The federal governance framework for AI remains fragmented. GAO determined that Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA established an AI Center of Excellence, achieving full implementation in selected areas. However, the Office of Management and Budget has not yet developed government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and the Office of Personnel Management has not established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. The Office of Science and Technology Policy did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements. This absence of consistent guidance means agencies cannot uniformly manage AI risks and benefits.

Internationally, governments are advancing policy frameworks through coordinated efforts. The OECD.AI policy observatory tracks over 900 national AI policies and initiatives and helps countries shape trustworthy AI aligned with the OECD AI Principles. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand to create an integrated partnership. Oxford Insights ranks national readiness on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption, providing cross-national comparisons of government AI maturity.

Legislative activity on AI is accelerating in the United States. Legislation tracked across 53 jurisdictions includes 3,803 AI bills. This volume of proposed law reflects the urgency governments feel to regulate AI, even as implementation within federal agencies remains nascent. Stanford HAI's AI Index monitors government and policy trends including legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, providing annual comprehensive analysis of AI's trajectory. The widening gap that Stanford HAI identifies between what AI can do and how prepared governments are to manage it applies directly to the federal sector, where safeguards remain under development despite the technology's rapid integration into operations.
